t: Cellars as heterotopias: domestic storage and the discursive-material politics of value
abs: This paper examines cellars as heterotopic sites for studying domestic waste management and the discursive production of value. Orienting to scholarship on materiality, space and affect, we conceptualize storage as a situated practice that endows space with social meaning and through which people enact particular identities and social values. Drawing on discourse-ethnographic data from cellar tours in four Swiss households, we present a mediated discourse analysis organized around four rhetorical tactics: erasure and deferral, relationalities, minimalism/excess and memory. These multimodal tactics help domestic actors negotiate competing value regimes and perform ‘good citizenship’ by managing clutter out of sight. We show how cellars conceal overflow to maintain curated domestic order and thereby, complicate social norms around tidiness and excess. We argue that cellars as heterotopias bend time–space relations and expose a discursive-material politics of value where storage practices index responsible citizenship and uphold social order. This renders the cellar simultaneously an ordinary infrastructure of domestic waste management and a micro-political site where negotiations around what – and who – holds value in society demand attention to waste as a matter of care.

t: News, elites and sex crimes: victim-blaming structures in media portrayals of Virginia L. Giuffre v Prince Andrew
abs: This paper considers media portrayals of the case of Virginia L. Giuffre v Prince Andrew as a means of exploring the hegemonising qualities of news discourse. Informed by theoretical accounts of hegemonic domination, news texts pertaining to the alleged sexual assaults of Virginia by Andrew are analysed using techniques and approaches from CDA. This reveals features that reinforce victim-blaming ideologies surrounding sexual violence, disinvite critical scrutiny of powerful societal institutions, and reflect a wider entrenchment of conservative ideology and intransigent masculinity in news production. The findings of the study contribute principally to feminist critical discourse studies and broader understandings of discursively enacted hegemony.

t: ‘I have no empathy’: self-Positioning in Israeli social media discourse during the Gaza war
abs: Israeli media have mostly avoided reporting on Palestinian suffering during Israel's assault on Gaza following the Hamas attacks of October 7, 2023. Social media thus became the main venue through which images of atrocities were circulated, serving as a summons to empathize with the Gazans' predicament. These calls were often rebuffed by empathy-blocking statements. In this study, we interrogate the discursive roles played by empathy-blocking acts, viewing them as a means through which Israelis position themselves within the wider debate over the country's actions in Gaza. We focus on denials of empathy towards Palestinians articulated on X (formerly Twitter), identifying three self-positioning functions. First, speakers may feel the need to justify their lack of empathy, thus signaling their engagement with the liberal moral order. Second, speakers may preface critiques of Israeli policies with ‘I have no empathy' statements, which serve as warrants positioning speakers as patriotic insiders entitled to voice critique. Third, blunt ‘I have no empathy' statements serve as a form of vice signaling, defiantly rejecting the liberal moral order. The affordances of X facilitate such discourse, due to the platform's privileging of negative sentiment, its role in reinforcing ingroup/outgroup boundaries and its championing of emotional authenticity.

This paper investigates a set of interactive resources for mining and energy education produced by the Australian mining industry and endorsed by Australia's Education Department. Building on Eaton, E., & Day, N. (2020. Petro-pedagogy: Fossil fuel interests and the obstruction of climate justice in public education. Environmental Education Research, 26(4), 457–473) ‘petro-pedagogy’, the study employs critical multimodal discourse analysis to show that these ‘Oresome interactives’, while often educational, disproportionately promote the interests of the mining industry. The resources represent the industry as an inevitable and positive part of modern Australian living, present the environmental impacts of mining as minimal and represent alternative energy sources as unstable, rare and unsightly. The paper concludes by calling for caution with regard to the use of such ‘gifted’ educational resources.

t: ‘I hate slavery, too’: a systemic functional linguistics analysis of pragerU’s history-based children’s programing
abs: We frame our study in a period of increased partisanship and polarization. This study examines Leo and Layla’s History Adventures, a web series produced by PragerU – a right-wing media organization approved for use in public schools in eleven U.S. states. Focusing on four episodes about enslavement and Reconstruction, we use Systemic Functional Linguistics (SFL) to analyze how verb processes position actors and ideologies within the narratives. Our findings reveal that adult voices dominate and are positioned as credible and knowledgeable figures, while child characters serve primarily to affirm authority and advance the narrative. Specifically, verb processes normalize, rationalize, and downplay the system of enslavement, portray white participants as moral agents, and minimize Black intellectual contributions. These narratives obscure systemic brutality and reproduce ideological distortions of U.S. history. We discuss implications to help students engage in language awareness in order to challenge historical narratives.

t: Non-discrete care: dialectical–relational CDA and the platformization of healthcare in Egypt
abs: This article examines Vezeeta, a leading Egyptian medical aggregator app, as a platformized site in which healthcare is reorganised through neoliberal discourse and interface governance. Drawing on Chouliaraki and Fairclough's dialectical-relational (DR) approach to critical discourse analysis, the study foregrounds the principle of non-discreteness, treating discourse as different from – yet inseparable from – material practice and institutional change. Conceptually, the article mobilizes orders of discourse to show how Vezeeta patterns and reorganizes discourses, genres, and styles in healthcare by mixing clinical and commercial genres, including menu-based ‘services,' discount banners, loyalty points, and swipeable ‘Featured Doctors' carousels. It then traces operationalization as the key mechanism through which dominant discourses are ‘put to work' in routines, identities, time-space coordination, and interactional norms, recasting patients as consumer-evaluators and doctors as competitive, reputation-managed service providers. The analysis demonstrates how market logics become institutionalized through metricized reputation (stars, visitor counts, tags), technologized evaluation templates, and synthetic personalization that frames platform monitoring as friendly support. Situated within Egypt's fragmented, largely out-of-pocket health economy and contemporary UHC reform discourse, the article argues that Vezeeta actively contributes to their materialization, producing stratified access, new norms of ‘good care,’ and platform-dependent forms of medical visibility and authority.

t: Constructing continuity: on the establishment of temporal legitimization in political discourse during the COVID-19 crisis
abs: This article investigates how political discourse during the COVID-19 crisis discursively constructs temporalities as a means of legitimizing crisis management. Building on Critical Discourse Studies and the Discourse-Historical Approach, it explores how continuity – often overlooked in crisis research – is not only maintained but actively constructed in discourse. Drawing on 28 Belgian governmental press conferences (2020 to 2022), the study identifies six discourses of continuity that were mobilized to justify measures, manage expectations, and synchronize collective action. Continuity unfolds in six discourses of the crisis: (1) maintaining the essentials, (2) the creation of habits in crisis, (3) the permanence of effort, (4) waiting as a tool, (5) projection in and out of the crisis and (6) predicting and progressing. These six discourses contrast with a view of continuity as inertia, as the absence of action or change. Instead, they articulate continuity at times as the maintaining force of a certain order, and at others as a creative force normalizing newness. The article argues that continuity, far from being inert, becomes a response to disruption, sustaining governance and order. Thereby, it contributes to the understanding of temporality as a central vector of legitimization in contemporary crises.

t: ‘Fighting corruption is not a beauty pageant’: discursive and rhetorical constructions of meritocracy and digital misogyny on Ghana’s ORAL task force
abs: This paper attends to the rhetorical and discursive constructions of gendered violence in Ghanaian digital culture surrounding the prospective nomination of women on Ghana’s ORAL task force – Operation Recover All Loot. As a charged rhetorical site of gendered and epistemic violence against women’’s acumen, this study unravels the deployment of meritocratic logics, ornamentalism, claims of intellectual ineptitude, tropes of competency, and tokenistic rhetorics to delegitimize women’s inclusion in high-stakes political offices in Ghana. Grounded in African Feminist Theory and Critical Discourse Analysis (CDA), this study evinces how public rhetors mobilize androcentric narratives on X to frame women as quintessential distractions and illegitimate political actors within anti-corruption initiatives. These discourses further establish a colonial gradient of neoliberalism, that constructs the political sphere as result-driven and inherently masculine, while co-naturalizing women as concerned with matters of beauty and aesthetics. The study calls for decolonial interventions nested within Indigenous public pedagogy and social media collective authorship for change.

t: From hegemonic consensus to polarisation: Austrian public discourse on Israel’s war in Gaza
abs: This article examines how Austrian public discourse on Israel’s war in Gaza shifted from hegemonic consensus to pronounced polarisation between October 2023 and September 2025. Drawing on a multi-domain corpus of political, media, and social media texts, and combining the Discourse-Historical Approach with Corpus-Based Narrative Analysis, the study triangulates representation, argumentation, and narrative to trace the evolution of antagonistic positions. The analysis shows how initial elite consensus in support of Israel fractured unevenly: political discourse remained unified longer, while media began to diverge earlier, and social media displayed polarisation from the outset. In line with Critical Discourse Studies, the paper highlights how polarisation is not simply a division of views but a discursive mechanism of power, silencing pro-Palestinian voices while legitimising hegemonic alignments. The study contributes methodologically by extending DHA with a systematic narrative dimension, bridging corpus-assisted and qualitative analysis to capture polarisation as a dynamic process. In doing so, it advances CDS debates on antagonistic binaries and demonstrates how hegemonic consensus can unravel into competing repertoires of legitimation, humanitarianism, and memory politics.

t: How to be a woman (in politics): constructions of gender in responses to Giorgia Meloni’s Instagram Posts
abs: Giorgia Meloni, leader of the Italian far-right party Fratelli d’Italia, is the first female Presidente del Consiglio in the history of Italy and is known to be vocal against feminism and gender-related issues. This unique scenario calls for an examination of gender from several perspectives; this paper focuses on users’ responses to Giorgia Meloni’s gendered posts (LGBTQIA + families, patriarchy, abortion, mansplaining) during the general election campaign in 2022. To situate the investigation, we engage with literature on far-right populism, (anti-)gender rhetoric, and online comments. Methodologically, we investigate six gendered posts by triangulating Corpus Assisted Discourse Studies and Feminist Critical Discourse Analysis. The examination of the language used stems from corpus-driven results, i.e. bigrams containing donna/e (woman/women) and expands to all the woman/women-forms in the corpus. The results of the six posts selected for the analysis present three main topics: construction of abortion, Meloni’s perceived engagement with other women, and descriptions of Meloni’s womanhood in politics. In connection with the last topic, the paper found that Instagram users conceptualize Meloni as an exceptional woman, a fighter against some gendered chaos, and, to a certain extent, a gentler extremist.

t: Metaphors of rupture, legitimization, and renewal in post-Assad Syrian leadership discourse
abs: This study examines the first 11 Arabic leadership speeches of Ahmad al-Sharaa, the former jihadist insurgent who became Syria’s transitional president after ousting Bashar al-Assad in 2024. Drawing on Critical Metaphor Analysis (CMA), the study analyzes how al-Sharaa employs metaphors to construct rupture with the Assad era, legitimize post-authoritarian leadership, and articulate political renewal. The analysis shows that al-Sharaa draws on metaphorical patterns typical of national and international post-conflict and post-revolutionary discourse to position himself as a pragmatic, collectivist, and service-oriented national leader rather than a jihadist one. The findings support core CMA claims by demonstrating how metaphors are used to persuade, manage accountability, and preserve face, particularly in contexts of evidential uncertainty. The findings also reveal that metaphor use varies with audience and communicative purpose, indicating a situationally adaptive rather than ideologically fixed discourse. As the first systematic analysis of al-Sharaa’s leadership discourse, this study establishes a baseline for tracking shifts in metaphorical framing and ideological positioning as his political authority consolidates.
